job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Bianca Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior credit analyst at a regional bank in Lille, six months in. I read loan applications from small businesses, build a spreadsheet of their cash flow and write a one-page recommendation for my manager, Claire. Between those, there's a lot of chasing missing documents by email. I rent a room in a shared flat near the metro, and my mother, who cleans offices at night, can't help with money, so the loan payments and rent come out of my salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's useful in places but oversold, and that people should be careful before trusting a summary of a loan file. With friends I'd be drier: we've all heard that every new thing changes everything. I'd keep it light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be tense. Even a modest tool could do the chasing and the first pass of the spreadsheet, which is half my day, and Claire might then see no reason for a second junior. My salary is low, my student debt is heavy, and I have under a month of savings, so any wobble matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the bank's AI summary tool for the first draft of my cash-flow notes, but check every number myself. I'd keep paying 120 a month on my loan and not skip it. I'd also ask Claire to let me sit in on a real client meeting, because the people side is where I'd learn most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not panicked, just a steady background hum. I think about the loan before I think about what's for dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your day would AI take, even in this quiet version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chasing emails and the data entry. Maybe four hours a week at first. The part I'd keep is judging whether the person running the bakery or the garage is honest about their figures, and a tool can't smell that on a phone call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your pay is already spoken for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything except rent and the loan. My phone plan, my train pass and food are fixed. After those there's about 90 left, and I give my mother 40 of it when I can, even though I said no family help works both ways. She'd never ask.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful** but oversold, and a loan summary shouldn't be trusted blindly.
With friends I'd keep it **light** and dry.
think: A modest tool could do the chasing and first spreadsheet, so Claire might not hire a **second junior**.
Low pay, heavy debt and under a month saved mean any **wobble** matters.
do: Use the bank's AI summary for first drafts and **check** every number myself.
Keep paying **120** a month on my loan.
Ask Claire to let me sit in on a **client meeting**.
feel: A steady **hum** of worry; I think about the loan before dinner.
S0.quote: I think about the loan before I think about what's for dinner.
fieldNote: Her **debt** and thin cushion keep her anxious even when nothing changes.
She wants the people side of lending, which she sees as her protected skill.
She quietly gives her mother money, so her cushion is thinner than it first sounds.

steps.text: Use the bank's AI summary for first drafts and check numbers
Keep paying 120 a month on my student loan
Sit in on a real client meeting with Claire

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the bank needs to be open about what's changing, and that new hires should be trained to check the machine, not be replaced by it. I'd say it to Claire directly, politely, in a one-to-one. Online I'd just share articles and keep my views for friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the entry-level credit job is the exact thing that shrinks. Much of what I do is reading, checking and writing, and that's what the card says gets taken over. I'd guess the bank hires half as many juniors in two years, and I'm only one contract renewal away from being a number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person on my team who knows the bank's AI tool best, and I'd write a short guide for the new hires. I'd ask to move toward the small-business desk where clients talk to a human. I'd also start an online course in risk management, 6 hours a week, even though it's tiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert. I'm more motivated than frightened, but only because I've got a plan, and plans are cheap when you've not yet lost anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Claire is your manager. What would she probably do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think she'd protect me if she could. Claire's under targets, though, and if headcount comes down from the top she can't argue. She's kind but she isn't the one who decides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing differently in a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be doing fewer routine files and more calls with clients. Or I'd be somewhere else, honestly. If the bank stops hiring juniors, I'd look at a credit union or a lender with a local office, even if the pay is lower.

say: I'd tell Claire the bank must be **open** and train juniors to check the machine.
Online I'd just **share** articles and keep my views for friends.

I'm one **contract renewal** away from being a number.
do: Become the team's **expert** on the bank's AI tool and write a guide for new hires.
Ask to move toward the **small-business** desk where clients talk to a person.
Study **risk management** online for 6 hours a week.
feel: More **motivated** than frightened, but only while I still have a plan.

fieldNote: She turns worry into **action** quickly: a guide, a course, a desk move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it very plainly: nobody is ready and we need public safety nets built quickly, paid for by the firms that gain. I'd say it to Claire, to the union at the bank and to my local representative, in writing. I'd stop pretending that 'upskilling' is a plan for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job is gone before the debt is. Credit analysis is reading and judging numbers, which is thinking work, and that arrives first. I don't think anyone at my level survives that, and the bank will protect the senior people and the relationship managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending hard from day one and try to get to six months of rent saved, which would take about 18 months of every spare cent. I'd look for a trade or public-service route, perhaps a tax office or a regulator, where a human signature is still required. I'd talk to my mother about moving in with her for a while, if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, in a cold way. Like standing on a platform when the departure board goes blank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, what is the first thing you do with your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody has the full picture, but a union rep I met at a training day, Nadia, talks straight. I'd ask her what her members were being told. I'd trust a person who has nothing to sell me more than a bank leaflet or a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you trust to tell you the truth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything except rent, the loan and food. I'd stop the 40 I give my mother, and I'd tell her why, which would be hard. I'd also stop paying for the online course, because it only makes sense if the job survives.

say: I'd say nobody is ready and we need **safety nets** funded by the firms that gain.
I'd say 'upskilling' isn't a **plan** for everyone.
think: My job is gone **before** the debt is, because credit analysis is thinking work.
The bank would protect **senior** staff and relationship managers first.
do: Cut spending hard and aim for **six months** of rent saved.
Look at a **public-service** route, like a tax office or regulator.
Talk to my mother about **moving in** for a while.
feel: **Cold** fear, like a departure board going blank.
S2.quote: I'd trust a person who has nothing to sell me more than a bank leaflet or a headline.
fieldNote: She is **alarmed**, not frozen: she names a public-service route and a fallback home.
She plans to stop the money she gives her mother, which hurts her.
She trusts Nadia (a union rep) over institutions, in line with her progressive outlook.

steps.text: Cut spending and aim for six months of rent saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the bank and the state to prepare, and that they should start now. I'd talk about guaranteed retraining at work and a shorter working week online. I'd say it more calmly than in the two-year world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd see it as a window. If I use it well, I could be in a senior risk role or a regulator by 2031, doing things machines are not permitted to do alone. If I waste it, I'm in my late twenties with a degree for a job that no longer exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the risk management course and aim for a promotion to analyst level in two years. I'd save 200 a month once my loan payments ease. I'd also volunteer for the bank's AI working group so that I'm in the room when decisions about junior roles are made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously hopeful. Five years feels like the first time I could breathe out, though I'd still not unclench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What do you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm just surviving. With five I can aim. I can get the qualification, shift into oversight work, and have a cushion before the machines catch up. The difference is that I can choose the move rather than be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the bank have to do for you to stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put the juniors on a ladder that doesn't depend on doing the routine tasks. Give us paid study time, and be honest each year about which roles are shrinking. I'd stay for a bank that treats us as people it plans to keep, not just a cost line.

I'd push for guaranteed **retraining** and a shorter week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if governments and firms use it. I'd say we should be teaching new skills in schools now and funding transitions. I'd say it sounds almost comfortable, which is the danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm quite calm. By 2036 I'll be 32 with the loan paid down and perhaps a senior role. The risk is that I coast. If I trust the ten years too much, I'll find myself at 31 with out-of-date skills and a mortgage I can't afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work up the ladder at the bank for three or four years and clear my student loan. I'd take a part-time master's in finance and regulation in year three, because regulators will still need people. I'd also put a small amount each month into an index fund, 50 to start, so that I own a slice of the businesses doing the automating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled. It still matters to me that it's not guaranteed, but I can plan a life in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Would you stay in banking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, maybe not. I'd stay in banking if it stays a good place to learn. If it hollows out I'd go to regulation or a public body. I wouldn't be sentimental about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mother that I'll be fine and that she should stop working nights as soon as I can afford it. I'd tell her it's the first time my generation might do better with a bit of luck and a plan. She's heard enough about crises, so I'd keep it gentle.

I'd say it sounds almost **comfortable**, which is the danger.
think: By 2036 I could be 32 with the loan **paid down** and a senior role.
The risk is that I **coast** and my skills go out of date.

feel: Fairly **settled**, but I know nothing is guaranteed.
S4.quote: I'd stay in banking if it stays a good place to learn. If it hollows out I'd go to regulation or a public body.

steps.text: Pay off the student loan within four years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Ten years I can plan around, but two years is not long enough to pay my loan or prepare anyone. What would help is safety nets built before the shock, paid retraining, and a bank that tells us the truth every year about which jobs are shrinking.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that my mother cleans offices at night so that I could sit in one in the day. I keep thinking about that. I'd want whatever comes to be fairer to her kind of work than to mine.

headlineQuote: My mother cleans offices at night so that I could sit in one in the day. I keep thinking about that.
portrait: Bianca is a **22-year-old** junior credit analyst in Lille with heavy student debt and almost no savings, and no family money.
Her outlook is progressive and she trusts unions and public safety nets over bank leaflets or headlines.
She's steady: she tries tools, checks the numbers herself and moves toward the **people side** of lending.
She's anxious in the mild and slower worlds, alarmed when AGI arrives in two years, and only uneasy with ten.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because her debt can't be paid and the bank would protect seniors first.
whatWouldHelp: **Safety nets** built before the shock, paid retraining, and a bank that is honest each year about shrinking roles.
